Compound interest is interest earned on interest. With simple interest you earn a return only on the money you deposited; with compounding, each interest payment is added to your balance and starts earning its own return. In the first few years the difference looks small, but because the growth is exponential it accelerates: at 7% a year, a balance doubles roughly every ten years, so $10,000 becomes about $20,000 after 10 years, $40,000 after 20 and $76,000 after 30 – without adding a cent.

Compounding frequency becomes meaningful when rates are high or balances are large: on $500,000 at 8 percent, daily versus annual compounding differs by about $1,600 a year. It also matters in reverse on debt. Credit cards usually compound daily, which is part of why balances grow faster than the headline APR suggests; the same calculator logic applies, just with you on the wrong side of it.

For a lump sum the formula is A = P(1 + r/n)<sup>nt</sup>, where P is the starting amount, r the annual rate as a decimal, n the number of compounding periods per year and t the number of years. GrowthCalc converts your rate to an effective monthly rate, (1 + r/n)<sup>n/12</sup> − 1, and then simulates every month: it applies that month's interest to the balance and adds your contribution at the start or end of the month. Summing those steps gives the exact result for both the initial deposit and the series of contributions.

For a lump sum the formula is A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where P is the starting amount, r the annual rate as a decimal, n the number of compounding periods per year and t the number of years. GrowthCalc converts your rate to an effective monthly rate, (1 + r/n)^(n/12) − 1, and then simulates every month: it applies that month's interest to the balance and adds your contribution at the start or end of the month. Summing those steps gives the exact result for both the initial deposit and the series of contributions.

For a single lump sum the classic formula is A = P(1 + r/n)nt, where P is the initial investment, r the annual interest rate as a decimal (7% = 0.07), n the number of compounding periods per year (365 daily, 12 monthly, 4 quarterly, 1 annually) and t the number of years. Dividing the rate by n and compounding n·t times is what turns a nominal 7% into an effective 7.23% when compounded monthly.

The difference between a standard savings account paying 0.5 percent and a high-yield account paying 4.5 percent is not a rounding error. On a $30,000 emergency fund it is more than $1,200 a year, for the same risk and the same insurance cover. A calculator turns that abstract percentage into a number you can act on.
The numbers at common rates

The preset assumes $15,000 already saved, $1,200 a month added, a 4.5 percent yield compounded monthly, and a five-year horizon. On those numbers the balance comes to just under $100,000 by the end of year five, close to a 20 percent deposit on a $500,000 home; adjust the figures to your market.

The preset below runs the pure lump-sum case: $10,000, no monthly contributions, 7 percent compounded monthly for 10 years. Add even $100 a month and the end balance jumps by more than $17,000, which is the second lesson of the page.

The preset is a plain, realistic case: nothing saved yet, $400 a month, 7 percent compounded monthly, 25 years. The result is a balance well over $300,000 from $120,000 of deposits. Change the monthly amount to see how linear the deposits are and how non-linear the growth is.

The preset models a $30,000 balance, $200 added monthly, 4.5 percent compounded daily (how most online banks credit interest) over three years, with inflation switched on at 3 percent so you can see whether the account is actually preserving purchasing power. Replace 4.5 with the APY you are being offered.

The preset sets GrowthCalc to daily compounding at 4.5 percent on a $20,000 balance with $250 added monthly over five years, a typical high-yield savings setup. Change the frequency select to monthly or annually and watch the final balance; the gap is smaller than most people expect.

The preset spreads the 2025 contribution limit of $7,000 across the year as $583 a month, starts from a $5,000 balance, assumes a 7 percent return compounded monthly over 35 years, and switches on a 3 percent inflation view. Adjust the monthly figure if you are over 50 and eligible for the catch-up contribution.

The preset starts at birth with $2,000, adds $300 a month, assumes a 6 percent return compounded monthly (a typical age-based 529 portfolio that gets more conservative as college approaches) over 18 years, and sets inflation to 5 percent to approximate tuition growth. The "in today's money" line tells you what the balance will buy in education terms.

The rule of 72 is a mental shortcut for how long money takes to double: divide 72 by the annual interest rate in percent. At 7% that gives roughly 10.3 years; at 10% about 7.2 years. The exact figure is ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + r), which GrowthCalc also shows. The rule is most accurate for rates between roughly 6% and 10%.

Three numbers matter more than the headline balance:

Time is the most powerful input in the formula. Imagine two people who both invest $300 a month at 7% until age 65. The one who starts at 25 contributes $144,000 over 40 years and ends with about $787,000. The one who starts at 35 contributes $108,000 over 30 years and ends with about $366,000. Waiting ten years cost only $36,000 in contributions but more than $420,000 in final balance – the lost decade was the one where the earliest deposits would have compounded the longest. Try it with the years slider: the final decade of any plan typically produces more growth than the first two combined.

With annual compounding interest is credited once a year; with monthly compounding one twelfth of the annual rate is credited every month and immediately starts earning interest itself. The more often interest compounds, the higher the effective annual yield, but the gap is modest: 7% compounded monthly equals an effective 7.23% per year, and daily compounding gives 7.25%. The length of time invested matters far more than the compounding frequency.

With daily compounding, the bank divides the annual rate by 365, applies that fraction every day, and the next day's interest is calculated on the slightly larger balance. The effective annual yield (APY) is (1 + r/365)<sup>365</sup> − 1. At a 4.5 percent nominal rate that is 4.60 percent APY; monthly compounding gives 4.59 percent; annual compounding gives exactly 4.50 percent. GrowthCalc simulates month by month using the effective monthly rate for the frequency you choose, so contributions are added every month regardless of how often interest is credited.

With inflation switched on, the calculator shows the balance in today's money. If the APY is below inflation, that line falls even as the nominal balance rises, which is the honest picture of a savings account in a high-inflation year. Interest is also usually taxable as income, so a 4.5 percent APY may be nearer 3.4 percent after tax for a mid-bracket saver.
